result.question: If hydrogen starts climbing on Transformer 1 at site MAIN, I want my operators to know what to suspect and what to check next. Using our known transformer failure modes, list every mode where rising hydrogen is a meaningful signal. For each one, say which one or two companion channels would confirm it, choosing from methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v and oti. Then look at the actual data between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 and tell me which of those modes the companion channels currently support. Run a DGA fault classification on the latest complete sample as a tie-breaker. Keep the list to the modes where hydrogen genuinely helps tell them apart, not every mode. If hydrogen didn't rise across the window, say so, but still give the watch-list, and label every mode as 'not currently indicated' rather than ranking them.
result.answer:
## Transformer 1 (MAIN): hydrogen watch-list, 15–18 Jan 2024

**Hydrogen did not rise across the window.** There are four daily samples (15, 16, 17 and 18 Jan; nothing on 19 Jan): **2845 → 2950 → 2800 → 2900 ppm**. That moves up and down within about ±4% and ends only +55 ppm (+1.9%) higher, with no steady upward trend. As you asked, every mode below is marked **not currently indicated** and none are ranked.

### Watch-list: modes where rising H₂ helps tell faults apart

| Failure mode | Why H₂ matters | Companion channels to confirm | 15–18 Jan status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Partial Discharge in Oil | H₂ is the main gas; the key test is methane staying low relative to H₂ (CH₄/H₂ < 0.1) | **methane** | Not currently indicated (CH₄/H₂ ≈ 2.5, far from a PD pattern) |
| Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking) | H₂ rises together with acetylene; C₂H₂/C₂H₄ > 1 | **acetylene, ethylene** | Not currently indicated (acetylene flat at 6–8 ppm) |
| High-Energy Arcing | H₂ and acetylene rise sharply; C₂H₂/C₂H₄ between 0.6 and 2.5 | **acetylene, ethylene** | Not currently indicated (C₂H₂/C₂H₄ ≈ 0.0004) |
| Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating (< 300 °C) | Moderate H₂ with methane leading; CH₄/H₂ > 1 separates it from PD | **methane, ethane** | Not currently indicated (methane flat at 7200–7406 ppm, ethane at 5400–5500 ppm) |
| Thermal Fault — Core/Winding (> 300 °C) | H₂ rises alongside a large ethylene rise; C₂H₄/C₂H₆ > 1 | **ethylene, ethane** (oti as a supporting check) | Not currently indicated (ethylene flat at 16,500–16,700 ppm, oti at 84–87 °C) |

I left out five modes because hydrogen doesn't help separate them. Cellulose insulation ageing is identified by co and co2. Oil contamination/moisture ingress and oil dielectric degradation are identified by dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v and dbds. Tap changer mechanical wear has no gas signature in the main tank.

### DGA fault classification (tie-breaker)
The DGA classification tool failed twice ("LLM unavailable"), so I have no tool result. I worked out the IEC 60599 ratios by hand from the latest complete sample (18 Jan):
- CH₄/H₂ = 7350/2900 ≈ **2.53**
- C₂H₂/C₂H₄ = 7/16600 ≈ **0.0004**
- C₂H₄/C₂H₆ = 16600/5450 ≈ **3.05**

These ratios fall in the **thermal fault, 300–700 °C (T2)** band, close to the T3 boundary. That points to the thermal side, not the discharge or arcing modes.

### Caveat
Even though nothing is trending, the gas levels themselves are very high: about 2,900 ppm H₂ and 16,600 ppm ethylene. That points to an existing thermal fault that has stopped developing, not a healthy unit. Operators should treat these levels as the baseline and act on any further rise in H₂, or any rise in acetylene (the arcing check) or ethylene (the thermal check). It's also worth confirming the levels with a lab oil sample.
